title: Naikon
summary: Naikon is a cluster name for long-running espionage activity that public reporting associates with China-nexus operators and describes as concentrated on government, military, and civil organisations around the South China Sea and wider Southeast Asia. Reporting describes spearphishing with malicious attachments and links, exploitation of web-facing services, and backdoor families that rely on living-off-the-land behaviour, including scheduled tasks, service creation, and legitimate command-line utilities, so that few files are dropped to disk. Some analyses argue the toolset is shared or rented rather than owned by one team, which makes the boundary between Naikon and neighbouring clusters genuinely contested. Defenders observe the activity through mail records, suspicious service and task creation, unusual process ancestry from web server software, and periodic beaconing to small hosting ranges. The common mistake is to hunt only for malware files. When the operator uses tools that already exist on the host, file-based detection has nothing to match, and behavioural baselines carry the detection load.

beginner.definition: Naikon is a research name for a cyber spying group that public reports link to China. It focuses on governments and armed forces near the South China Sea. It often uses tools that already exist on the victim computer.
beginner.whyItMatters: Because the attackers use normal system tools, antivirus alerts may never fire. The activity looks similar to routine administration work. That makes it easy to miss and hard to prove later. If you have no baseline of normal behaviour, you cannot spot the odd job. Careful logging of system changes is often the only reliable clue.
howItWorks: The attackers pick targets that already hold valuable political or military information.
They send a message with a file or link shaped around that interest.
After getting in, they create a scheduled job so their code restarts.
They use tools already installed on the system to avoid new files.
A quiet connection to their server lets them send commands and collect the files.
They keep the access open and return whenever they need more data.
beginner.example: Picture a cleaner who works in an office tower and uses only the supplies already in each room. He never carries a bag, so the security desk has nothing unusual to check. He moves between floors using the staff lift, and he leaves everything exactly as he found it. Weeks pass before anyone notices that a filing cabinet has been read. An intruder who lives off the land behaves the same way. There is no suspicious object to find, only ordinary tools being used at odd times and in odd places.
takeaways: Attackers can work without ever installing a harmful file.
Scheduled jobs and new services are worth watching closely.
You need a record of normal activity before you can spot the odd.

objectives: Explain what living-off-the-land means and why it defeats file-based detection.
Describe how scheduled tasks and services provide persistence on a host.
Identify process ancestry anomalies that reveal web-facing exploitation.
Explain why behavioural baselines are necessary for detecting tool-reuse intrusions.
Discuss why shared tooling makes group boundaries in public reporting uncertain.
Describe the data sources that support hunting for this activity.
